intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that cerebellar ataxia, impaired intellectual development, and dysequilibrium syndrome-4 (CAMRQ4) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the ATP8A2 gene (605870) on chromosome 13q12.

paragraphs.text: Cerebellar ataxia, impaired intellectual development, and dysequilibrium syndrome-4 (CAMRQ4) is an autosomal recessive disorder. It is characterized by cerebellar ataxia, impaired intellectual development, dysequilibrium, and cerebellar atrophy, and some patients walk on all fours (quadrupedal locomotion) (Onat et al., 2013). Onat et al. (2013) described cerebellar ataxia, mental retardation, and dysequilibrium syndrome as rare and genetically heterogeneous. Severity varies. Some patients have severe hypotonia, involuntary movements, and severe developmental delay (Mohamadian et al., 2020; Narishige et al., 2022). Others have congenital ataxia with near normal cognition (Damasio et al., 2021).

paragraphs.text: Mohamadian et al. (2020) reported 3 affected sibs of Arab descent from an Iranian family. Their parents were healthy first cousins. The proband was a 9-year-old girl. Her first noticeable sign was severe neonatal hypotonia, and all her psychomotor and developmental milestones were then delayed. She used a wheelchair and could not walk, sit, or hold her head up, and she had had feeding difficulties since infancy. Her affected brother and sister, aged 17 and 15 years, had features similar to the proband's. All 3 patients had IQs of 20 to 40, delayed speech and language, dysarthria, absent deep tendon reflexes, and cerebellar atrophy on MRI. Hearing examination showed no significant impairment. The proband had normal metabolic investigations, no seizures, and no optic atrophy.

paragraphs.text: Narishige et al. (2022) reported 2 Japanese sibs who developed athetotic movements at 1 and 2 months of age. They also had ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, feeding difficulty, hypotonia, and severely delayed development. One of them had retinal degeneration and optic atrophy. Over time both lost their tendon reflexes (areflexia) and developed flattened auditory brainstem responses. At last follow-up, neither patient could sit or control the head, although some nonverbal communication remained.

paragraphs.text: Ozcelik et al. (2008) studied 4 large consanguineous Turkish kindreds with quadrupedal gait. In 2 of the families the trait mapped to chromosome 9p24 and was caused by mutations in the VLDLR gene. In the other 2 families the phenotype was not linked to chromosome 9p. The authors concluded that hereditary disorders with quadrupedal gait in humans are genetically heterogeneous. In a reply to Herz et al. (2008) and Humphrey et al. (2008), Ozcelik et al. (2008) again addressed the genetic heterogeneity of cerebellar hypoplasia with quadrupedal locomotion.

paragraphs.text: Gulsuner et al. (2011) studied a large consanguineous Turkish family with quadrupedal locomotion, mental retardation, and cerebrocerebellar hypoplasia. The disorder was linked to a 7.1-Mb region of homozygosity on chromosome 17p13.1-p13.3. Diffusion-weighted imaging and fiber tractography showed abnormalities of the cerebellum and corpus callosum, in particular atrophy of the superior, middle, and inferior cerebellar peduncles. Morphometric abnormalities of the precentral gyrus and of Brodmann areas BA6, BA44, and BA45 were also reported. The authors sequenced the whole homozygous region in 3 affected individuals and 2 obligate carriers. This identified a private homozygous P856L missense mutation in the WDR81 gene (614218), which cosegregated with the disorder in the extended family. The mutation lies in a highly conserved region of WDR81, between the N-terminal BEACH domain and the C-terminal WD40 beta-propeller domains. WDR81 was highly expressed in the cerebellum and corpus callosum, especially in the Purkinje cell layer. Gulsuner et al. (2011) stated that WDR81 was the third gene implicated in human quadrupedal locomotion, after VLDLR and CA8.

paragraphs.text: Mohamadian et al. (2020) identified a homozygous c.1339G-A transition in the ATP8A2 gene in 3 affected sibs from a consanguineous Iranian family with CAMRQ4. The mutation results in a gly447-to-arg (G447R) substitution. Both parents and 2 healthy sibs were heterozygous, and 1 healthy sib carried 2 normal copies of the gene. The variant was not found in public databases or in 100 ethnically matched controls, and it was classified as likely pathogenic by ACMG criteria. Gly447 lies in a highly conserved part of the cytoplasmic N (ATP-binding) domain. Homology modeling predicted that the substitution greatly reduces protein stability and changes the ligand-binding pocket.

paragraphs.text: Onat et al. (2013) identified a homozygous ile376-to-met (I376M) missense mutation in the ATP8A2 gene in a consanguineous Turkish family. Four members of the family had cerebellar ataxia, mental retardation, dysequilibrium, cerebellar atrophy, and quadrupedal locomotion (CAMRQ4). The variant was found by targeted next-generation sequencing and was supported by segregation analysis, population screening, and prediction programs. It lies in a highly conserved C-terminal transmembrane region of the E1-E2 ATPase domain.

paragraphs.text: Mohamadian et al. (2020) identified a homozygous c.1339G-A transition in the ATP8A2 gene in 3 sibs with CAMRQ4 from a consanguineous Iranian family of Arab descent. The mutation results in a gly447-to-arg (G447R) substitution. The patients had IQs of 20 to 40, dysarthria, absent deep tendon reflexes, and cerebellar atrophy. Both parents and 2 healthy sibs were heterozygous. The variant was not found in public databases or in 100 ethnically matched controls. Gly447 lies in a highly conserved part of the cytoplasmic N (ATP-binding) domain, and homology modeling predicted that the substitution reduces protein stability.
